explanation: The X1908+075 orbit was identified before the Swift and MAXI surveys. The measured period agrees with the published 4.400-day clock.
The recurrent X-ray outbursts of 1A 0535+262 trace the published approximately 111-day binary orbit. The timing literature identifies the same clock before either monitor survey.
The BAT source H 1538−522 is the eclipsing binary 4U 1538−522. Its orbit accounts for this peak.

decision: Daily sampling alias of a published orbit
explanation: Daily averaging reflects the second harmonic of the 3.728-day orbit into the search band. Native-cadence fits in BAT and MAXI both prefer the published orbit to 2.1572 days over the full span and in each half.
EXO 1657−419 is OAO 1657−415. Its eclipse ephemeris accounts for the observed period.
This transient's previously published 18.5482-day orbital recurrence agrees with the BAT and MAXI measurements.
SS 433 has a long-established spectroscopic jet-precession clock. Published timing gives 162.375 days, consistent with the independently detected X-ray modulation.
The bright eclipsing binary Cen X-3 has a published orbital ephemeris. A single best-fitting period over the survey averages over secular evolution.

decision: Consistent with the fifth orbital harmonic
explanation: Multiplying 49.78679 days by five gives 248.934 days. Published X-ray outburst timing gives 248.78 days and also detects the half-orbit harmonic. The BAT spectrum contains additional harmonics of the longer orbit. A distinct 49.8-day clock is unnecessary to explain these measurements.
The published timing ephemeris of EXO 2030+375 gives an approximately 46-day orbit. The cadence of X-ray outbursts can vary in orbital phase.

decision: Consistent with the second orbital harmonic
explanation: The 7.184-day signal is close to half the published 14.365-day orbit. BAT monitoring has previously shown two flares per orbit, near periastron and apastron.
4U 1820−30 has a documented evolving superorbital cycle. The published change from approximately 171 to 167 days includes the modulation found here.

decision: Daily sampling alias of a published orbit
explanation: The one-day reflection of Her X-1’s 1.700167-day orbital frequency lies at 2.42823 days. The orbit wins the native-cadence comparison in the full light curves and in both halves of each instrument.
The recovered fundamental agrees with the published orbital ephemeris of the eclipsing binary SMC X-1.

decision: Daily sampling alias of a published orbit
explanation: The daily peak is the one-day reflection of the second harmonic of the 3.89-day SMC X-1 orbit. Both instruments recover the orbital period in their native-cadence fits and prefer it in both halves.
2S 0114+650 is also known as 3A 0114+650. Published spectroscopy gives an 11.5983-day orbital clock.
The approximately 30.75-day clock is the established superorbital modulation of 2S 0114+650. It is distinct from this system’s 11.6-day orbit.
This is the eclipsing binary EXO 1722−363. Its published 9.7403-day orbit agrees with the independent BAT and MAXI measurements.
This is the previously measured superorbital cycle of LMC X-4. Long-baseline monitoring gives 30.32 ± 0.04 days.

decision: Daily sampling alias of a published orbit
explanation: Reflecting the known 1.408379-day orbital frequency about one cycle per day reproduces this peak. Native BAT and MAXI prefer the 1.408-day orbit over the 3.449-day daily solution in both halves.
Previously published eclipse timing gives 6.07413 ± 0.00004 days. The present measurement recovers the same orbit.
